props.title: My Man Godfrey
props.initialSlug: Hobo butler teaches wealthy family about humanity

sections.content: My Man Godfrey (1936) revolutionized screwball comedy with its razor-sharp critique of Depression-era class dynamics. William Powell's sophisticated performance as Godfrey, a "forgotten man" turned butler, plays brilliantly against Carole Lombard's dizzy socialite Irene Bullock. The film's genius lies in how director Gregory La Cava uses madcap comedy to smuggle in serious social commentary about wealth inequality and human dignity. The Bullock mansion becomes a microcosm of 1930s America, with Godfrey navigating between the frivolous rich and his fellow homeless men at the city dump.

sections.content: The film's influence echoes through decades of social satire, from The Palm Beach Story (1942) to Trading Places (1983). La Cava's masterful direction keeps the pace brisk while allowing moments of genuine pathos to land. The party scenes, with their choreographed chaos and rapid-fire dialogue, became a template for depicting high society's absurdity. Eugene Pallette and Alice Brady deliver exceptional supporting performances as the bewildered father and scattered mother, perfecting character types that would become screwball staples.

What sets My Man Godfrey apart is its sophisticated handling of class consciousness. Unlike later films like Sullivan's Travels (1941), Godfrey isn't a rich man slumming it to learn about life - he's a former wealthy man who chose to live among the forgotten, giving him unique insight into both worlds. The film's art deco sets by Charles D. Hall create a stunning visual contrast between the dump and the mansion, while maintaining a consistent sense of unreality that enhances the social commentary. SUBHEAD: Depression-Era Social Commentary in Comedy

sections.content: The film's treatment of the Depression stands unique among its contemporaries. While Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933) and Modern Times (1936) addressed economic hardship directly, My Man Godfrey uses the screwball format to make its points with sophistication and wit. The scavenger hunt sequence that opens the film - where wealthy partygoers treat finding a "forgotten man" as a game - remains one of Hollywood's most incisive critiques of privilege.
